title: Popular navigation apps unlikely to ditch Mercator maps despite UN resolution
gist: The UN General Assembly passed a non-binding resolution (164 in favor, US the only opposing vote) encouraging governments and tech companies to adopt equal-area map projections like Equal Earth instead of the size-distorting 16th-century Mercator projection, but Google Maps (2+ billion monthly users) and Apple Maps are expected to keep using Mercator because of its practical navigational advantages, with research suggesting Mercator familiarity measurably worsens people's size perception of countries and continents.

themes.theme: The UN resolution and its limits

insights.claim: A UN General Assembly resolution promoting equal-area world maps passed 164 votes in favor with six abstentions on September 4, with the United States the sole country voting against it, calling it a 'radical ideological project.'
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Near-unanimous international consensus against sole US opposition on a cartography-equity issue signals the resolution carries diplomatic/symbolic weight even though it imposes no binding requirements.
insights.locator: described it as a “radical ideological project”

insights.claim: The non-binding UN resolution imposes no map changes on anyone; it only encourages governments, schools, international organizations, and technology companies to use the Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps when relative size matters.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Because the resolution is purely advisory, near-term commercial impact on mapping/navigation products is expected to be minimal — a useful expectation-setter against overreacting to headline coverage of the vote.
insights.locator: The non-binding UN resolution does not impose map changes

themes.theme: Why navigation apps will keep Mercator

insights.claim: Google Maps and Apple Maps, the most widely used navigation apps — Google Maps alone has more than 2 billion monthly users — still use variations of the Mercator projection and are unlikely to abandon it despite the UN resolution, because Mercator's straight-line compass-bearing property remains uniquely practical for real-world navigation.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A clear, low-ambiguity prediction that the world's two dominant consumer navigation platforms (with a combined multi-billion user base) will not change their default map projection despite the political symbolism of the UN vote.
insights.locator: the UN resolution is unlikely to change how millions of people

insights.claim: The Mercator projection, created by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569, was designed to show straight lines matching a ship's constant compass bearing, making it a genuinely practical maritime and digital-navigation tool — the very property the UN resolution's backers themselves acknowledged as useful.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Explains the underlying causal reason Mercator persists in navigation software specifically (versus education/media), clarifying that the debate is really about context-appropriate map use, not a simple right/wrong choice.
insights.locator: His focus was on creating a map projection that showed straight lines

themes.theme: Documented perceptual and geopolitical distortion effects

insights.claim: The Mercator projection artificially enlarges landmasses farther from the equator, causing Africa to appear roughly the same size as Greenland on the map despite being about 14 times larger in reality.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A concrete, memorable quantified distortion example (14x) useful for framing the practical stakes of map-projection choice in media and education.
insights.locator: leads to absurdities such as the continent of Africa

insights.claim: A study published in Communication Reports found that pairing national-security arguments with a Mercator map could influence how people evaluated the Trump administration's proposal to purchase Greenland, suggesting Mercator's visual size inflation of Greenland has real geopolitical persuasion effects.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Direct empirical evidence that map-projection choice measurably shapes public opinion on real foreign-policy proposals, not just an abstract aesthetic/educational debate.
insights.locator: The visually inflated size of certain landmasses

insights.claim: A study of 130,000 people found that greater familiarity with the Robinson map projection (a compromise between equal-area and shape accuracy) was associated with more accurate estimates of country/region/continent sizes than greater familiarity with the Mercator projection.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Large-sample empirical evidence directly linking habitual map exposure to measurable geographic-size misperception, the core scientific justification underlying the UN resolution's push for alternative projections.
insights.quote: This result emphasizes the need to use less area-distorted map projections in, for example, (social) media and in educational materials
insights.locator: the researchers wrote in their paper
